words.definition: Pleased about something.
words.example: I am glad you came.
words.whyHere: The mildest word: a small, quiet feeling of pleasure.

words.definition: Feeling pleasure or good about life.
words.example: She felt happy at the party.
words.whyHere: Stronger and more general than 'glad': a clear, warm good mood.

words.definition: Very pleased and full of joy.
words.example: He was delighted to win.
words.whyHere: Much stronger than 'happy': joy that plainly shows.

words.definition: Extremely pleased and excited.
words.example: We were thrilled by the news.
words.whyHere: The peak here: happiness so big it feels like excitement.

words.definition: To find something pleasant.
words.example: I like this old song.
words.whyHere: The mildest: a small, positive feeling.

words.definition: To get pleasure from something.
words.example: We enjoy long evening walks.
words.whyHere: Stronger than 'like': active, felt pleasure.

words.definition: To care about or like something very much.
words.example: They love classic films.
words.whyHere: Much stronger than 'enjoy': a deep, warm feeling.

words.definition: To love someone or something very deeply.
words.example: Fans adore the young singer.
words.whyHere: The peak: the strongest, most devoted liking.

reviewNote: furious vs enraged is close; enraged implies loss of control. Supported by Cambridge/Oxford learner definitions.

words.definition: Slightly angry or impatient about something.
words.example: I was annoyed when the bus arrived late again.
words.whyHere: The mildest word here: a small irritation that you can usually control.

words.definition: Feeling strong displeasure toward someone or something.
words.example: She was angry that nobody had told her about the change.
words.whyHere: Stronger than 'annoyed': the feeling is clear and hard to ignore.

words.definition: Extremely angry.
words.example: He was furious when he saw the damage to his car.
words.whyHere: Much stronger than 'angry': the emotion is intense and often shows in your face.

words.definition: Made extremely angry, often to the point of losing self-control.
words.example: The crowd was enraged by the unfair decision.
words.whyHere: The peak of the scale: anger so strong that it takes over.

reviewNote: enormous vs gigantic are close; gigantic suggests almost unimaginable size.

words.definition: Larger than the usual size.
words.example: They live in a big house.
words.whyHere: The mildest: simply larger than normal, nothing extreme.

words.definition: Extremely large.
words.example: A huge crowd filled the square.
words.whyHere: Much bigger than 'big': the size really stands out.

words.definition: Very large in size or amount.
words.example: The company made an enormous profit.
words.whyHere: Stronger than 'huge': far beyond ordinary size.

words.definition: So large it is hard to imagine.
words.example: A gigantic wave hit the shore.
words.whyHere: The peak: giant-like size at the top of this scale.

reviewNote: concerned vs worried overlap; concerned is often milder and more measured.

words.definition: A little worried about something.
words.example: Parents are concerned about the exam.
words.whyHere: The mildest: mild, thoughtful worry.

words.definition: Feeling that something bad may happen.
words.example: She was worried about the results.
words.whyHere: Clearer worry than 'concerned'.

words.definition: Very worried and uneasy.
words.example: He felt anxious before the interview.
words.whyHere: Stronger than 'worried': tense, restless worry.

words.definition: So worried that you cannot stay calm.
words.example: They grew frantic when the child vanished.
words.whyHere: The peak: panicky worry that takes over.

words.definition: To look quickly at something.
words.example: I often glance at the clock.
words.whyHere: The mildest: a fast, brief look that is soon over.

words.definition: To turn your eyes toward something.
words.example: Please look at the board now.
words.whyHere: A normal, neutral act of seeing, longer than a glance.

words.definition: To look steadily for a long time.
words.example: They often gaze at the stars.
words.whyHere: Stronger than 'look': a long, often admiring or thoughtful look.

words.definition: To look directly for a long time, often rudely.
words.example: It is rude to stare at people.
words.whyHere: The most intense: a fixed, hard look that others notice.

reviewNote: brilliant vs dazzling is close; dazzling adds the sense of briefly overwhelming the eyes.

words.definition: Not giving much light.
words.example: The dim lamp barely lit the room.
words.whyHere: The lowest on the scale: faint, weak light.

words.definition: Giving out plenty of light.
words.example: The kitchen is bright and sunny.
words.whyHere: Clearly lit: a normal, healthy level of light.

words.definition: Very bright and shining.
words.example: The brilliant sunshine filled the valley.
words.whyHere: Stronger than 'bright': light that shines and stands out.

words.definition: So bright it briefly hurts the eyes.
words.example: The dazzling lights made her blink.
words.whyHere: Stronger than 'brilliant': bright enough to overwhelm the eyes for a moment.

words.definition: So bright you cannot see.
words.example: A blinding flash filled the sky.
words.whyHere: The peak: light so intense it stops you seeing at all.

reviewNote: nervous vs scared boundary is soft; nervous leans toward mild anxiety.

words.definition: Slightly worried or afraid about something.
words.example: I feel nervous before tests.
words.whyHere: The mildest: a little unease rather than real fear.

words.definition: Afraid of something.
words.example: The dog was scared of thunder.
words.whyHere: Clear fear, stronger than 'nervous'.

words.definition: Very afraid because of something sudden or serious.
words.example: The loud bang left them frightened.
words.whyHere: Stronger than 'scared': a sharper, bigger fear.

words.definition: Extremely afraid.
words.example: She was terrified of the dark.
words.whyHere: The peak: fear so strong it can freeze you.

words.definition: To speak very quietly using breath, not the voice.
words.example: Please whisper in the library.
words.whyHere: The quietest: barely any sound at all.

words.definition: To speak in a low, soft voice.
words.example: He began to murmur a reply.
words.whyHere: A little louder than a 'whisper', but still soft.

words.definition: To say something very loudly.
words.example: Do not shout in class.
words.whyHere: Much louder than a 'murmur': a raised, forceful voice.

words.definition: To shout as loudly as you can.
words.example: Coaches often yell from the sideline.
words.whyHere: The loudest: a sharp, full-force shout.

words.definition: Light rain with very fine drops.
words.example: A light drizzle fell all morning.
words.whyHere: The mildest: barely enough rain to notice.

words.definition: A short period of rain.
words.example: A sudden shower soaked the garden.
words.whyHere: More rain than a 'drizzle', but usually brief.

words.definition: A heavy fall of rain.
words.example: The downpour flooded the streets.
words.whyHere: Much heavier than a 'shower': rain that pours down.

words.definition: A very large, sudden flood of water.
words.example: The deluge swept away the bridge.
words.whyHere: The peak: rain so heavy it causes flooding.

reviewNote: gust is a burst rather than a sustained wind; ranked by peak force above breeze.

words.definition: A gentle, light wind.
words.example: A gentle breeze cooled the beach.
words.whyHere: The mildest: soft moving air that feels pleasant.

words.definition: A short, sudden rush of wind.
words.example: A sudden gust knocked the sign over.
words.whyHere: Stronger than a 'breeze': a brief but forceful burst.

words.definition: A very strong wind.
words.example: A fierce gale tore off roof tiles.
words.whyHere: Much stronger than a 'gust': a steady, powerful wind.

words.definition: A period of violent weather with strong wind.
words.example: The storm raged through the night.
words.whyHere: Stronger than a 'gale': wind with rain and real danger.

words.definition: An extremely violent storm with very strong winds.
words.example: The hurricane destroyed homes on the coast.
words.whyHere: The peak: the most destructive wind on this scale.

reviewNote: glum vs sad is close; glum stresses a quiet, moody low rather than intensity.

words.definition: Quietly sad and low in mood.
words.example: He looked glum after the loss.
words.whyHere: The mildest: a gentle, low mood rather than deep pain.

words.definition: Unhappy.
words.example: She felt sad when they left.
words.whyHere: A clear unhappy feeling, stronger than 'glum'.

words.definition: Very unhappy.
words.example: The rain made the campers miserable.
words.whyHere: Much stronger than 'sad': unhappiness that fills you.

words.definition: Feeling great sorrow, usually from loss.
words.example: She was heartbroken by the news.
words.whyHere: The peak: deep sorrow, often after losing someone or something.

reviewNote: excellent, outstanding and superb are very close; ranked by how far each rises above the norm.

words.definition: Of a fair or pleasing standard.
words.example: It was a good meal.
words.whyHere: The mildest: acceptable and pleasing, nothing special.

words.definition: Very good.
words.example: The film was great fun.
words.whyHere: Clearly better than 'good'.

words.definition: Extremely good.
words.example: She did an excellent job.
words.whyHere: Stronger than 'great': very high quality.

words.definition: So good it clearly stands out from the rest.
words.example: His work was truly outstanding.
words.whyHere: Stronger than 'excellent': better than almost all others.

words.definition: Of the very highest quality.
words.example: The orchestra gave a superb performance.
words.whyHere: The peak: about as good as something can be.

words.definition: To eat something in small bites.
words.example: Mice nibble on cheese at night.
words.whyHere: The mildest: tiny, slow bites.

words.definition: To take food into the mouth and swallow it.
words.example: We eat lunch at noon.
words.whyHere: The plain, neutral word for taking food.

words.definition: To eat quickly and greedily.
words.example: Hungry kids gobble their food fast.
words.whyHere: Stronger than 'eat': fast, greedy eating.

words.definition: To eat all of something quickly and hungrily.
words.example: Wolves devour their prey quickly.
words.whyHere: The peak: eating everything fast and eagerly.

reviewNote: famished, ravenous and starving are all very close; ranked by increasing severity per learner dictionaries.

words.definition: Slightly hungry.
words.example: I feel peckish before dinner.
words.whyHere: The mildest: only a little hungry.

words.definition: Wanting or needing food.
words.example: The children are hungry after school.
words.whyHere: The normal word: a clear need to eat.

words.definition: Very hungry.
words.example: By noon we were famished.
words.whyHere: Stronger than 'hungry': an uncomfortable, strong hunger.

words.definition: Extremely hungry.
words.example: After the hike he felt ravenous.
words.whyHere: Stronger than 'famished': hunger that feels urgent.

words.definition: Suffering or weak from a serious lack of food.
words.example: The lost hikers were starving.
words.whyHere: The peak: the most extreme hunger on this scale.
